newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke accuses Labour of copycat tactics.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke accuses Labour of copycat tactics.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke accused the opposition Labour Party on Thursday of copycat tactics.
In an interview with the Times newspaper he said Labour were fighting an American-style campaign, striking attitudes rather than putting forward policies.

With an unfortunate slip of the tongue, Clarke hinted he expects his Conservative Party to lose a looming general election. The Times said he began talking of "when" Labour gets in to power, before quickly correcting himself to "if they get in."
An election must be held by May 22 but Prime Minister John Major is believed to favour May 1.
"If the economy is doing well, get as close to the government as you can sound on economic policy. Enter into no commitments," was Clarke's view of Labour's election strategy.

And the day after the Conservative's faultline over Europe gaped open again, Clarke -- widely seen as the most pro-European member of the government -- said it was quite likely a single European currency would be delayed beyond its scheduled start dat of January 1, 1999.

On Wednesday, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told BBC radio that on balance the government was "hostile" to European economic and monetary union (EMU). Clarke later dismissed the comments as a "slip of the tongue".
Overnight, the two ministers issued a joint statement to Reuters saying there was no change to the government's wait-and-see policy over European economic and monetary union.
In his Times interview, Clarke said shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown's proximity to him on a whole swathe of economic issues did not neutralise the economy as an election issue.

He said there was growing disenchantment with Labour's refusal to flesh out policies, particularly on the planned windfall tax on privatised utilities, and its failure so far to nail down an explicit inflation target.
"I think the key thing when fighting an election is firstly to set out your genuine intentions and secondly to create a climate in which you are able to deliver those intentions," Clarke said.

If Labour does win the election it would have difficulty in controlling public finances, Clarke said, but he admitted that Brown would face no overwhelming need to raise interest rates to ward off inflationary pressure.
